source_cards.front: What does right-of-way decide, and what should you never assume?
source_cards.back: Right-of-way decides who proceeds first and who waits, especially where drivers or pedestrians meet without signals or signs, and you should never assume the vehicle on the right automatically goes first.

source_cards.front: Who still in the intersection must you yield to?
source_cards.back: Yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and drivers who are still in the intersection.

source_cards.front: At a four-way stop, who goes first, and who wins a tie?

source_cards.front: At a four-way stop, when does the driver on the right go first?
source_cards.back: At a four-way stop, arrival order decides who goes, and the driver on the right wins only as the tie-breaker when drivers arrive at the same moment.

source_cards.front: At an uncontrolled intersection with no signs or signals, whom do you yield to?
source_cards.back: At an uncontrolled intersection with no signs or signals, yield to vehicles approaching from your right.

source_cards.front: Whom do you yield to at a roundabout and at an uncontrolled T-intersection?
source_cards.back: Yield to traffic already circulating in a roundabout, and to cross traffic at an uncontrolled T-intersection.

source_cards.front: How does yielding at an uncontrolled T-intersection differ from an uncontrolled crossroads?
source_cards.back: Yielding to the vehicle on your right is the rule for an uncontrolled intersection, but at an uncontrolled T-intersection you yield to the cross traffic.

source_cards.front: Entering a roundabout, which vehicles do you yield to?
source_cards.back: Entering a roundabout, the vehicles you yield to are the ones already circulating inside it.

source_cards.front: What must you do for a pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane?
source_cards.back: Yield to a pedestrian who uses a guide dog or carries a white cane even if that person is not in the intersection, stopping at least ten feet away until the person has left the roadway.

source_cards.front: Does a blind pedestrian keep the right-of-way outside the intersection?
source_cards.back: A blind pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane keeps the right-of-way even outside the intersection, and you must stop at least ten feet away until the person clears the road.

source_cards.front: Which vehicles must you yield to when passing, turning left or hearing sirens?
source_cards.back: Yield to a vehicle passing you on either side in your direction, to oncoming vehicles when you turn left or make a U-turn, and to emergency vehicles using lights or sirens.

source_cards.front: Turning left or making a U-turn, whom do you yield to?
source_cards.back: Turning left or making a U-turn, you yield to oncoming vehicles, and you also yield to any vehicle overtaking you on the left or the right.

source_cards.front: What counts as an intersection?
source_cards.back: An intersection is any place where two paths cross, which includes cross streets, driveways, parking lot entrances and railroad crossings.

source_cards.front: What should you check before entering an intersection?
source_cards.back: Before entering an intersection, look left and right, make sure no vehicles or pedestrians are in it, and check for a clear path to where you are going.

source_cards.front: What should you do when you cannot see well into an intersection?
source_cards.back: If you cannot see well into an intersection, edge forward carefully and stay ready to brake, especially where there are no signals or signs.

source_cards.front: What can hide cross traffic as you approach an intersection?
source_cards.back: Trees, buildings and parked vehicles can hide cross traffic, so approach a blocked intersection slowly.

source_cards.front: Why should you search left, right and left again even with the right-of-way?
source_cards.back: Because some drivers miss or ignore signs and signals, search left, right and left again before crossing, even when you have the right-of-way.

source_cards.front: What room do you need before passing, and must others move over?
source_cards.back: Pass only when there is enough room in front of the vehicle you are passing, and remember that other drivers are not required to move over for you.

source_cards.front: Does passing change the speed limit or require the other driver to move over?

source_cards.front: Which arm position means a left turn, a right turn, and slowing or stopping?

source_cards.front: What should you do before any turn?
source_cards.back: Before any turn, check your mirrors, your surroundings and your blind spot, stay in your lane, signal your turn and yield the right-of-way.

source_cards.front: How do you set up a left turn at an intersection?
source_cards.back: For a left turn, check that your path is clear, keep near the center line, watch for pedestrians crossing on the left, and wait about halfway into the intersection while leaving room for oncoming turners.

source_cards.front: What is a U-turn, and is it always safe?
source_cards.back: A U-turn is one smooth U-shaped motion that reverses your direction, and it can be very dangerous even though some intersections allow it.

source_cards.front: In what order do you signal and move, and how early do you signal before an intersection turn?
source_cards.back: Turn on your signal, check around you, and then move; at an intersection, begin signaling about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, before the turn.

source_cards.front: When your turn comes just after an intersection, when do you signal?
source_cards.back: When your turn comes just after an intersection, wait until you have crossed the intersection before signaling.

source_cards.front: How does signal timing differ for a turn at an intersection and a turn just past one?
source_cards.back: At an intersection you signal about three seconds, roughly one hundred feet, ahead of the turn, but for a turn just past an intersection you wait until you have crossed it.

source_cards.front: What must you avoid during a turn, and why give trucks and buses room?
source_cards.back: Do not change lanes in the middle of a turn or cut across the center line, and leave extra room for trucks and buses, which may swing over the center line as they turn.

source_cards.front: Which lane is for going around slower vehicles on a multi-lane road, and why is passing on the right risky?
source_cards.back: On a multi-lane road the left-most lane is the lane for going around slower vehicles, and passing on the right is risky because the other driver may not see you.

source_cards.front: How does a normal pass differ from going around on the shoulder?
source_cards.back: Passing on the left is the normal pass, while going around on a paved shoulder is allowed only past a stopped or left-turning vehicle.

source_cards.front: What must you do before changing lanes?
source_cards.back: Before changing lanes, make sure the way is clear, signal first, move only one lane at a time, and look over the shoulder on the side you are moving toward.

source_cards.front: Why are mirrors not enough before a lane change?
source_cards.back: Checking mirrors is not enough before a lane change, because the blind spots are seen only by looking over the shoulder toward the new lane.

source_cards.front: When is it safe to return to the driving lane after passing?
source_cards.back: It is safe to return to the driving lane once both headlights of the vehicle you passed appear in your rearview mirror.

source_cards.front: What cue tells you it is safe to move back after passing?
source_cards.back: After passing, the cue that it is safe to move back into the driving lane is seeing both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.

source_cards.front: How far and how fast should you back up?
source_cards.back: Because it is hard to see behind a vehicle, back up as little as possible and no faster than a slow walk.

source_cards.front: What should you do after backing, and what if you miss an exit?
source_cards.back: After backing, scan left and right before rejoining traffic, and if you miss an exit or turn, never back up; continue to the next exit and come back.

source_cards.front: You miss your highway exit. What do you do?
source_cards.back: A missed exit is handled by driving to the next exit and coming back, never by backing up on the road.

source_cards.front: What should you watch for, and how big a space do you need, to parallel park?
source_cards.back: For parallel parking between vehicles, watch for traffic, pedestrians and fixed objects, and look for a space about three-six feet longer than your vehicle.

source_cards.front: How does parallel parking begin?
source_cards.back: Parallel parking starts with your turn signal on and a stop alongside the vehicle ahead of the space, about two feet away from it.

source_cards.front: How does the starting gap compare with the extra length of the space?
source_cards.back: When you begin parallel parking you stop about two feet from the car ahead, and the space you choose should be about three-six feet longer than your car.

source_cards.front: What is the next step after stopping beside the car ahead?
source_cards.back: Next, turn the wheel fully toward the side you are parking on, left for the left side of the road and right for the right side, and back up slowly.

source_cards.front: When do you turn the wheel the other way while parallel parking?
source_cards.back: Once your bumper clears the vehicle in front, turn the wheel sharply the other way and back slowly until you are parallel to the curb.

source_cards.front: How do you finish a parallel park, and what distances should you end with?
source_cards.back: Finish by straightening the wheels, ending about a foot from the curb and at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind.

source_cards.front: How does the final curb distance compare with the distance from other vehicles?
source_cards.back: At the end of a parallel park you should be about a foot from the curb, but at least two feet from the vehicles ahead and behind.

source_cards.front: Which hill-parking case turns the wheels left, and which cases turn them right?
source_cards.back: Uphill with a curb is the left-wheel case, while uphill without a curb and every downhill park are right-wheel cases.

source_cards.front: What should you watch for, and how big a space do you need, to parallel park?

source_cards.front: A bus swings over the center line as it turns. May you do the same?

source_cards.front: How should your wheels point while you wait to turn left, and why?
source_cards.back: While waiting to turn left, keep the steering wheel and wheels straight, because if you are hit from behind with the wheel turned left you will be pushed into oncoming traffic.

source_cards.front: What is a U-turn, and is it always safe?
source_cards.back: A U-turn is one smooth U-shaped motion that reverses your direction, and it can be very dangerous even though some intersections allow it.

source_cards.front: What should you check before making a U-turn?
source_cards.back: Before a U-turn, check all mirrors and traffic and look for any sign that prohibits it.

source_cards.front: When is a U-turn allowed on a rural two-lane highway?
source_cards.back: On any rural two-lane highway a U-turn is allowed as long as it is done safely and does not interfere with traffic.

source_cards.front: How is a U-turn made, and where is it allowed unless a sign forbids it?
source_cards.back: A U-turn is a single continuous motion and is allowed on any rural two-lane highway when safe, unless a sign forbids it.

source_cards.front: With multiple turn lanes, which lane should you finish the turn in?
source_cards.back: With multiple turn lanes, finish the turn in the matching lane: start in the left-most lane and end in the left-most lane, start in the middle and end in the middle.

source_cards.front: From which lane must you turn right on a four-lane roadway?
source_cards.back: When turning right from a four-lane roadway, the turn must be made from the lane closest to the right curb or road edge.

source_cards.front: What is the second step of a Y-turn?
source_cards.back: Y-turn step two is to signal left, check your blind spot, turn left across to the opposite curb and stop.

source_cards.front: When may you use a paved shoulder to get around a vehicle?
source_cards.back: You may use a paved shoulder to get around a vehicle only when that vehicle is stopped or is making a left turn.

source_cards.front: When may hand signals replace turn signals, and what are the three signals?
source_cards.back: Hand signals may replace turn signals that are missing or hard to see: arm straight out the driver window to turn left, elbow bent with the hand up to turn right, and hand pointed down to slow or stop.

source_cards.front: Which arm position means a left turn, a right turn, and slowing or stopping?
source_cards.back: In hand signals a straight arm means a left turn, an arm bent upward means a right turn, and an arm pointed down means slowing or stopping.

source_cards.front: What is the blue Report Problem or Emergency sign for?

source_cards.front: What does a Slippery When Wet sign tell you to do?
source_cards.back: A Slippery When Wet sign means the pavement ahead may be slick, so reduce your speed.

source_cards.front: What does a Signal Ahead sign warn about?
source_cards.back: A Signal Ahead sign warns of traffic lights ahead, so be prepared to slow and stop.

source_cards.front: What does a Lane Ends sign show, and what should you do?
source_cards.back: A Lane Ends sign shows which lane is ending; move into the remaining lane once it is safe.

source_cards.front: What does a Curved Road sign warn about?

source_cards.front: How does a Sharp Turn sign differ from a Curved Road sign?
source_cards.back: A Sharp Turn sign can point left or right and asks you to be ready to slow for the turn, unlike a Curved Road sign, which marks a gradual bend.

source_cards.front: What does a Hill sign warn of?

source_cards.back: Reduced Speed Ahead is a regulatory sign meaning you should slow down because a curb or slippery road might lie ahead.

source_cards.front: When does a school zone speed limit apply?
source_cards.back: On a school zone speed limit sign, the posted speed may not be exceeded whenever children can be seen.

source_cards.front: How do brown guide signs differ from green ones?
source_cards.back: Green and brown guide signs both give directions to places, but the brown ones point to fun or scenic places such as parks.

source_cards.front: What does an Interstate highway sign look like?
source_cards.back: An Interstate highway sign is a shield, red on top and blue on the bottom, with white lettering.

source_cards.front: What does a county road sign look like?
source_cards.back: A county road sign is a white rectangle with rounded edges and black letters.

source_cards.front: What does a state road sign look like?
source_cards.back: A state road sign is shaped like a milk jug with its spout at the bottom and is white with black letters.

source_cards.front: What does the round yellow railroad warning sign tell you?
source_cards.back: The railroad advance warning sign is round and yellow with an X symbol and black letters, telling you a crossing is ahead and to watch for a train.

source_cards.front: At a crossbuck with flashing lights, when may you go?
source_cards.back: At a crossbuck with flashing lights, the lights flash when a train approaches from either direction; wait until they stop and the track is clear before going.

source_cards.front: How does the round railroad warning sign differ from the crossbuck?
source_cards.back: The round yellow railroad warning sign with an X tells you a crossing is there, while the white X-shaped crossbuck also lists how many tracks you will cross.

source_cards.front: What do the Tracks out-of-service and Exempt plaques mean?
source_cards.back: A Tracks out-of-service sign means the tracks are no longer used, while an Exempt sign means only certain vehicles are excused from stopping before crossing.

source_cards.front: What kind of signal do many country intersections have?
source_cards.back: Many intersections out in the country have only a single yellow or red light.

source_cards.front: How do you treat an intersection whose traffic light has no power?
source_cards.back: If a traffic light has no power or is not working properly, treat the intersection as if it had a stop sign.

source_cards.front: How must every turn on red begin and end?
source_cards.back: Any turn on red starts with a full stop; then yield to all traffic and complete the turn staying in your lane.

source_cards.front: What does a steady yellow light mean, and what should you do?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow light means red is coming, so slow down and stop before you enter the intersection.

source_cards.front: What should you do if the light turns yellow while you are already in the intersection?
source_cards.back: If the light turns yellow while you are already in the intersection, do not stop; keep going through.

source_cards.front: How does a steady yellow differ from a flashing yellow?
source_cards.back: A steady yellow means stop before the intersection if you have not entered it, while a flashing yellow means slow down and proceed with caution.

source_cards.front: On a steady green light, whom must you still yield to?
source_cards.back: A steady green light lets you go through the intersection, but you must still yield to emergency vehicles and others the law requires.

source_cards.front: The light turns green while you are stopped. What do you wait for?
source_cards.back: If you were stopped and the light turns green, let cross traffic clear the intersection before you go.

source_cards.front: When may you turn left on a steady green light?
source_cards.back: On a steady green you may turn left only when it is safe, because oncoming traffic has the right-of-way.

source_cards.front: How does a left turn on a green ball differ from one on a green arrow?
source_cards.back: On a steady green ball a left turn must yield to oncoming traffic, while under a green arrow no oncoming or crossing traffic should be moving.

source_cards.front: Does a green light or green arrow mean you never yield?

source_cards.front: Where are crosswalks found?

source_cards.front: What do the solid white edge line and the yellow line on your left mark?
source_cards.back: A solid white line marks the right edge of the travel lane, and a solid or dashed yellow line marks the left edge of the lanes going your way.

source_cards.front: When may you cross a solid white line between lanes?
source_cards.back: A solid white line between lanes may not be crossed except to avoid a hazard or when you are turning within the next block.

source_cards.front: How does crossing a dashed white line differ from a solid white line?
source_cards.back: A white dashed line may be crossed when safe, while a solid white line between lanes may be crossed only for a hazard or a turn within the next block.

source_cards.front: Where should you stop at a crosswalk?
source_cards.back: At a crosswalk, stop with your front wheels just short of the solid white line and never stop on the crosswalk itself.

source_cards.front: What do solid yellow lines separate, and what do two of them mean?
source_cards.back: Solid yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, and two solid yellow lines mean neither direction may pass.

source_cards.front: When may you cross a double solid yellow line to turn?
source_cards.back: You may cross a double solid yellow line to turn into a driveway when it is safe.

source_cards.front: When may you cross a double yellow to pass, and when may you not?
source_cards.back: You may also cross it to pass a vehicle moving at less than half the speed limit when safe, but not if that vehicle is farm equipment.

source_cards.back: The double yellow exceptions are turning into a driveway and passing a vehicle going under half the speed limit, and the second never applies to farm equipment.

source_cards.front: How does a single dashed yellow line differ from a double solid yellow?
source_cards.back: A single dashed yellow line allows passing when safe, while two solid yellow lines forbid passing from either side.

source_cards.front: With a dashed line beside a solid yellow line, who may pass?
source_cards.back: Where a dashed yellow line runs beside a solid one, only drivers on the dashed side may pass.

source_cards.front: With mixed yellow lines, which line decides whether you may pass?
source_cards.back: With a dashed line beside a solid yellow line, the line nearest you decides: dashed on your side allows passing, solid on your side does not.

source_cards.front: When may you cross the solid yellow line into a shared center lane?
source_cards.back: You may cross the solid yellow line into a shared center lane to make a left turn or U-turn, but only enter it when it is safe.

source_cards.front: What is a flex lane, and when is it open?
source_cards.back: On some highways signs allow the paved shoulder to be used as a flex lane, which is separated by a solid yellow line and opened according to traffic volume and special events.

source_cards.back: Seat belts keep you positioned to control the vehicle, help prevent injury in a crash and help keep you from being thrown out.

source_cards.back: Adjust the belt so your fist fits between it and your chest, and never tuck the shoulder belt under your arm or let it hang loose over your arm.

source_cards.back: The lap belt goes low across the hip bones, while the shoulder belt crosses the chest with about a fist of room.
